opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when I was deciding, Stanford's robotics community felt small but really exciting. It wasn't a huge, centralized robotics program like some other places. It was more a handful of groups across computer science, mechanical engineering, and aeronautics, each doing pretty different things. Some labs focused on manipulation and control, others on perception, planning, or human-robot interaction.

What drew me in was the overlap with computer vision and machine learning. Around that time, deep learning was transforming vision, and people at Stanford were starting to ask what it would mean for robots. Could robots learn from data the way vision models learned from ImageNet? That question felt wide open, and Stanford seemed like one of the few places where you could be right at that intersection, with people who deeply understood learning and people who deeply understood robots.

There was also a culture of being ambitious and a bit unconventional. Nobody told you to work on a problem because the field had always done it that way. You were encouraged to think about the big picture: what would make robots truly general and useful in the real world? For a young PhD student, that freedom was very appealing, even if it also meant figuring out a lot on your own.

So I saw it less as an established robotics powerhouse and more as a place where something new was forming. I wanted to be part of building it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Stanford’s robotics community felt “small” when he was deciding where to do his PhD, describing it as a handful of groups rather than a large, centralized program.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, when I was deciding, Stanford felt less like a single lab and more like an ecosystem. You had people working on robot learning, on perception, on manipulation, on human-robot interaction, and they were all within a short walk of each other and actually talked to one another. That mattered to me because I didn't want to be boxed into one narrow framing of what robotics research was.

The other thing I noticed was how much the community sat at the intersection of robotics and the broader AI world. Computer vision and machine learning were exploding at the time, and at Stanford those weren't separate departments down the hall. Robotics students were in the same reading groups, the same classes, and sometimes the same projects as the vision and learning people. I had a sense that the interesting problems in robotics were going to come from pulling those fields together, and Stanford seemed like a place where that was already happening naturally rather than something you had to fight for.

And I'll admit the culture played a part too. The students I met during visit days were ambitious but not cutthroat. People seemed genuinely curious about each other's work. For a PhD, where you're going to spend five or six years with these people, that counted for a lot.

r001.rationale: The response describes Stanford as a broad, nearby, collaborative ecosystem, but does not say Danfei Xu perceived its robotics research community as unusually small.

astra-6.text: I saw Stanford as a place where I could explore robotics from a lot of different angles. I was interested in the intersection of robotics and AI, so having a community where people approached those problems from different perspectives was really appealing. I wanted an environment where I could learn broadly and figure out which questions I really wanted to work on.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes Stanford’s robotics community as offering varied perspectives, but does not say Danfei Xu viewed it as unusually small.
